title: Kotlin coroutines on the server
scopeHtml: Server-side concerns only: dispatchers, blocking calls, framework support, context propagation, cancellation, fan-out/timeouts/bulkheads, coroutines vs virtual threads, testing, production bugs. Coroutine mechanics (state machines, Job internals) are owned by A1.

questions.promptHtml: On a Kotlin backend, what are Dispatchers.Default, Dispatchers.IO and Dispatchers.Unconfined, and how do you pick one for a request handler?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Wrong dispatcher choice is the number one source of coroutine latency bugs. They want to see you know what each pool is for and how big it is.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Default is for CPU-bound work and has as many threads as cores (minimum 2). IO is for blocking calls like JDBC or file IO and by default allows max(64, cores) concurrent blocking tasks. They share one underlying thread pool. Unconfined runs wherever the caller resumed and I basically never use it in server code. For a handler I run suspend code from non-blocking clients on whatever dispatcher the framework gives me, and wrap each blocking call in withContext(Dispatchers.IO).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Coroutines are not threads; a dispatcher decides which thread runs the code between suspension points.

Dispatcher Backed by Parallelism Use for
Default shared scheduler cores, min 2 CPU work: JSON mapping, hashing, compression
IO same scheduler, elastic max(64, cores), property kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism blocking JDBC, files, legacy SDKs
Unconfined caller thread, then whichever thread resumes it n/a rare; tests, special event-loop code
Main UI thread 1 not present on servers

Default and IO share threads, so withContext(Dispatchers.IO) from a Default coroutine usually does not even switch threads (best effort, per the API docs). The IO limit is a cap on concurrent blocking tasks, not a cap on threads created, which is why you can add views on top of it (see Q220).

Key rule: a suspend function that calls a non-blocking client (Ktor client, WebClient awaitBody, R2DBC) needs no dispatcher switch. A suspend function that wraps blocking code must switch itself, so callers never need to know (main-safety).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Main-safe: callers can invoke from any dispatcher
class UserRepo(private val ds: javax.sql.DataSource) {
    suspend fun find(id: Long): User? = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        ds.connection.use { c ->
            c.prepareStatement("select id,name from users where id=?").use { ps ->
                ps.setLong(1, id)
                ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> if (rs.next()) User(rs.getLong(1), rs.getString(2)) else null }
            }
        }
    }
}
data class User(val id: Long, val name: String)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running JDBC on Default: 8 cores means 8 blocked coroutines stall all CPU-bound work too.
  • Using IO for CPU work "to be safe": it gives 64 threads fighting over 8 cores, adding context switches.
  • Assuming IO has exactly 64 threads; it is a concurrency cap of max(64, cores).
  • Using Unconfined in handlers; resumption thread becomes unpredictable (could be a Netty event loop).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does withContext(IO) always switch threads? → No; if already on the shared scheduler it tries to stay on the same thread, best effort.
  2. How big is Default on a 2-core container? → 2 (minimum 2). Containers with CPU limits: the JVM sees the cgroup limit, verify your JDK version honours it.
  3. Where does the IO 64 limit come from and can you change it? → System property kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism, read at startup; usually better to add limitedParallelism views per dependency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "IO for network and disk, Default for compute." Senior adds the shared-pool detail, the 64 cap versus pool size on 4-core pods, main-safe suspend APIs, and that the right IO size is derived from the downstream connection pool, not guessed.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service moved JSON parsing to Dispatchers.IO "because it is a request path" and saw p99 rise during traffic peaks from CPU oversubscription; moving it back to Default fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: What does Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n) do, how is it different from a fixed thread pool dispatcher, and how would you size it for a service with a 20-connection HikariCP pool?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that dispatcher limits are the first bulkhead and must match downstream capacity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: limitedParallelism(n) returns a view that lets at most n coroutines of that view run at once, reusing the parent's threads. On Dispatchers.IO the views are elastic: their sum is not capped by IO's 64, so each dependency gets its own independent limit. For a 20-connection Hikari pool I would use a view of about 20, equal to the pool size, so excess coroutines queue in the dispatcher (cheap) rather than blocking threads waiting on getConnection.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• A view caps concurrently running coroutines, not threads. Threads are borrowed from the parent and are not dedicated.
  • Views are independent and need no closing. The docs' example: three views of 100, 60 and 64 can run 224 blocking tasks at peak, while steady state shares few threads.
  • Versus newFixedThreadPoolContext(n) / Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n).asCoroutineDispatcher(): that creates n dedicated threads you must close, and idle ones stay alive. A view creates no new pool.
  • limitedParallelism(1) gives serial execution with happens-before between sections, but it is not a mutex: a suspended coroutine releases the slot and others interleave.
  • Sizing with Little's law: concurrent in-flight = throughput x latency. At 400 RPS with 25 ms queries that is 400 x 0.025 = 10 connections busy on average. Pool 20 gives 2x headroom. The dispatcher view should not exceed the pool, otherwise threads block in getConnection (default connectionTimeout 30 s in HikariCP, verify for your version) and you waste them.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
object Dispatch {
    val db = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "db")        // = Hikari maximumPoolSize
    val payments = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(30, "pay-sdk")
}
suspend fun <T> dbCall(block: () -> T): T = withContext(Dispatch.db) { block() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking limitedParallelism(1) protects shared mutable state across suspension points; it does not.
  • Creating a view per request (cheap, but then each has its own limit and nothing is limited). Make views singletons.
  • Sizing view larger than the connection pool and moving the queue into Hikari where it times out noisily.
  • Using newFixedThreadPoolContext without closing it (leaks threads on redeploy).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Do the views' limits add up to a limit on IO? → No, IO views are elastic; the sum is not capped by IO's own parallelism.
  2. How is that different from a Semaphore? → Semaphore limits coroutines across suspension points (including time spent suspended on non-blocking calls); a dispatcher view limits only coroutines currently running on a thread.
  3. When would you still use a dedicated thread pool? → Isolation of a misbehaving blocking library, or thread-affine native code; a view shares the underlying pool so a leaked blocked thread still counts globally.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use limitedParallelism to limit threads." Senior: ties the number to downstream pool and Little's law, knows the elastic IO semantics, and knows it is not a mutex.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team capped everything at the default 64 IO, while the DB pool was 10; 54 threads sat in getConnection, starving unrelated HTTP calls that shared IO.

questions.promptHtml: Why is calling a blocking function from a coroutine dangerous, and what are the options when you must call blocking code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core server-side coroutine hazard. They want the cause (few threads, many coroutines) and the remedies.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A coroutine suspension frees the thread, but a blocking call holds it. The dispatcher has few threads (cores for Default, or Netty's small event-loop set), so a handful of blocked coroutines can freeze everything on that dispatcher. Options: wrap in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a limitedParallelism view, use a non-blocking client, or on JDK 21+ run the blocking code on virtual threads. runBlocking inside a coroutine is the worst option.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Threads are the scarce resource: 8-core Default has 8 threads. If 8 coroutines call Thread.sleep(2000) or JDBC, nothing else on Default runs for 2 s even though CPU is idle. Symptoms: low CPU, rising latency, healthy-looking GC.
  • Netty event loop (Ktor/WebFlux) is worse: typically cores x 2 threads (verify per server), shared by all connections. One blocked loop thread stalls every connection assigned to it.
  • Detection: BlockHound (agent that throws on blocking calls in non-blocking threads), thread dumps where Default workers show Thread.State: RUNNABLE inside socket read, kotlinx debug mode, or JFR socket-read events.
  • withContext(IO) moves the block to a pool designed for it. It does not make the call non-blocking, it just moves the cost.
  • runBlocking inside a coroutine blocks the carrier thread until the inner finishes and can deadlock if the inner needs the same thread.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: blocks a Default/event-loop thread
suspend fun price(id: String): Money = legacySdk.fetchPrice(id)

// Fixed
suspend fun price(id: String): Money = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { legacySdk.fetchPrice(id) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking suspend means non-blocking; the modifier only permits suspension.
  • Blocking inside synchronized or Thread.sleep instead of delay.
  • runBlocking in a request path "just to call a suspend function".
  • Wrapping a blocking call in async with no dispatcher switch and expecting parallelism.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you find blocking calls in a running service? → BlockHound in tests, thread dumps of Default workers, JFR, async-profiler wall-clock mode.
  2. Is delay safe? → Yes, it suspends and frees the thread.
  3. Is blocking inside Dispatchers.IO free? → No, it still occupies one of the capped slots; you must size it against downstream capacity.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use withContext(IO)." Senior explains the thread math, event-loop impact, BlockHound, and that the move to IO shifts the bottleneck to the IO cap and downstream pool.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A migration to WebFlux plus coroutines kept an old blocking S3 client call in a handler; one slow S3 region froze the event loops and health checks timed out.

questions.contextHtml:
Ktor service, 4-core pods (2 GB RAM), 600 RPS peak. After shipping a new /orders/{id} endpoint, p99 goes from 80 ms to 9 s during a downstream blip, CPU stays at 15%, heap is fine, no GC pauses over 20 ms. Health checks (/health, pure in-memory) start timing out. The code:

get("/orders/{id}") {
    val id = call.parameters["id"]!!
    val order = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
        ordersDao.find(id)            // blocking JDBC, Hikari max pool 10
    }
    val items = coroutineScope {
        (1..5).map { async { runBlocking { itemsClient.get(order, it) } } }.awaitAll()
    }
    call.respond(Response(order, items))
}

jstack shows 4 DefaultDispatcher-worker-N threads in HikariPool.getConnection or inside runBlocking/socket read.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs, explain the symptoms, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more threads" or "increase the Hikari pool". It misses that CPU is idle because threads are blocked, and that runBlocking inside async is the multiplier.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is itemsClient blocking or suspend (decides whether runBlocking is even needed)? Which engine (Netty/CIO)? Hikari connectionTimeout? Did the downstream latency change? Are health checks on the same dispatcher?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load or roll back the endpoint; set a timeout on itemsClient; lower request concurrency at the load balancer so queues drain.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) JDBC on Default starves 4 workers; (b) runBlocking in async blocks a worker per item call, so one request pins up to 5 threads; (c) Hikari pool of 10 and 4 threads blocked in getConnection; (d) GC (ruled out by logs); (e) network (red herring, it only triggers the stall).
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack/jcmd <pid> Thread.print three times 5 s apart: same worker threads stuck; async-profiler wall-clock mode (-e wall); Micrometer Hikari metrics hikaricp.connections.pending; BlockHound in an integration test.
  5. Root cause: Default has 4 threads. Blocking JDBC and runBlocking park all four, so any coroutine on Default, including the health check, cannot run. CPU is idle because threads are waiting on IO, not computing.
  6. Fix: Short-term: move DAO to a bounded IO view; replace runBlocking with a suspend client call. Long-term: non-blocking driver or virtual threads for the blocking leg.
val db = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(10, "db")
get("/orders/{id}") {
    val order = withContext(db) { ordersDao.find(call.parameters["id"]!!) }
    val items = coroutineScope { (1..5).map { async { itemsClient.get(order, it) } }.awaitAll() }
    call.respond(Response(order, items))
}
  1. Prevention: BlockHound in CI, a lint/detekt rule banning runBlocking outside main/tests, per-dependency dispatcher views, alert on hikaricp.connections.pending > 0 for 1 min, and a separate dispatcher for health checks.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just raise the Default size; that hides the issue and starves CPU work. I would not raise Hikari to 100 without checking DB max connections across all pods.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if itemsClient is a blocking Java SDK only? → wrap it in withContext of its own bounded view, and add timeout and circuit breaker.
  • Would virtual threads fix this? → For the blocking legs yes, but you still need timeouts and bounds on the DB pool.
  • Why did health checks fail but the CPU stay at 15%? → they were queued behind blocked workers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An endpoint that passed all tests failed in prod only when a vendor slowed down. The team had been tuning GC for two days; one jstack showed every worker in the same socket read.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests more RAM/cores or tuning GC; cannot explain idle CPU.
  • Hire: identifies blocking on Default and runBlocking, moves to IO with a limit.
  • Strong hire: ties limits to Hikari pool, adds BlockHound/detekt guards, separates health check, discusses virtual threads trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: How does Spring support Kotlin coroutines in controllers, and what differs between running them on Spring MVC and on WebFlux?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many Kotlin shops run Spring; interviewers check whether you know which thread your suspend controller runs on and what libraries are needed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With kotlinx-coroutines-core and kotlinx-coroutines-reactor on the classpath, Spring lets @RestController methods be suspend or return Flow, and coRouter for functional endpoints. Spring adapts the coroutine to a Mono/Flux internally. On WebFlux it runs on the Netty event loop, so any blocking there is fatal. On MVC the suspend method is run through async request handling; I would verify on my Spring version which thread executes it and keep blocking work behind withContext(IO) either way.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Per the Spring docs: Mono<Void> maps to suspend fun, Mono<T> to suspend fun: T, Flux<T> to Flow<T>. Controllers can return Deferred, Flow, or suspend results; Flow is push-based with backpressure via suspension.
  • Transactions are not @Transactional ThreadLocal based in reactive mode: use TransactionalOperator.executeAndAwait or Flow.transactional. The Spring docs list this approach for coroutines.
  • Tracing: the observation lives in a ThreadLocal or Reactor Context; suspend code needs PropagationContextElement (Micrometer context-propagation) or Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation().
  • Filters: CoWebFilter for WebFlux. Error handling: @ExceptionHandler works with suspend methods.
  • WebFlux: few threads, so blocking JDBC must be offloaded. MVC: thread-per-request model; suspend controllers still fine for parallel fan-out but the benefit is smaller.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@RestController
class OrderController(private val client: WebClient, private val repo: OrderRepo) {
    @GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
    suspend fun order(@PathVariable id: Long): OrderView = coroutineScope {
        val o = async { repo.find(id) }                       // suspend, non-blocking driver
        val p = async { client.get().uri("/price/$id").retrieve().awaitBody<Price>() }
        OrderView(o.await(), p.await())
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting kotlinx-coroutines-reactor; coroutine support silently does not activate.
  • Using @Transactional on suspend methods in a non-reactive setup and expecting thread-bound transactions to follow the coroutine across threads.
  • Blocking JDBC (JPA) inside a WebFlux suspend controller without withContext.
  • Assuming MDC and security context follow automatically.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How is Flow returned over HTTP? → Adapted to Flux; with JSON array or SSE/NDJSON depending on media type.
  2. What does suspend add over returning Mono? → Imperative code, structured concurrency with coroutineScope, normal try/catch.
  3. If the client disconnects mid-request, is your coroutine cancelled? → Spring cancels the subscription, which cancels the coroutine (reactive path); see Q228.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "You just add suspend." Senior: dependencies, Mono/Flux mapping, which thread executes, transaction and context propagation differences, and the migration trap of mixing JPA with WebFlux.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An MVC to WebFlux port using Spring Data JPA in suspend controllers made latency worse; every query blocked a Netty thread.

questions.promptHtml: At a high level, how does Ktor use coroutines to handle requests, and what should you know before putting blocking or long-running work in a route?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks a mental model of a coroutine-native server instead of memorizing syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Ktor runs on an engine (Netty, CIO, Jetty, Tomcat). Each request is handled in a coroutine, and route handlers are suspend lambdas, so non-blocking calls free the thread while waiting. Plugins (formerly features) form a pipeline around handlers. Blocking calls must be moved off the engine threads with withContext. Request coroutines are tied to the call; work launched into an application-level scope outlives the request.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Pipeline: request goes through plugins (auth, content negotiation, status pages, call logging) then the route handler, in the call's coroutine context. Exceptions map via StatusPages.
  • Engine: with Netty the engine uses its own event loop groups to accept/read; Ktor dispatches handler work to its call-processing coroutine pool. Exact thread counts are configurable in engine config (callGroupSize etc.); verify for your Ktor version.
  • The Ktor HTTP client is also suspend-based, so fan-out is coroutineScope { async { client.get() } }.
  • Lifetime: application has a scope; launch long-lived background work there (or a managed scope) and cancel it on shutdown (ApplicationStopping).
  • Timeouts: use the HttpTimeout plugin on clients, withTimeout in handlers, and engine-level request timeouts.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun Application.module() {
    routing {
        get("/profile/{id}") {
            val id = call.parameters["id"]!!
            val (user, prefs) = coroutineScope {
                val u = async { userClient.get("http://users/$id").body<User>() }
                val p = async { prefsClient.get("http://prefs/$id").body<Prefs>() }
                u.await() to p.await()
            }
            call.respond(Profile(user, prefs))
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Launching GlobalScope.launch in a route for "fire and forget" (no cancellation, lost errors).
  • Blocking JDBC/file IO directly in the handler.
  • Creating a new HttpClient per request (connection pool and thread leak); share one and close at shutdown.
  • Assuming a client disconnect always cancels the handler; engine-dependent, verify.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does background work started by a request belong? → In an application-scoped CoroutineScope with SupervisorJob and explicit shutdown, not in the call.
  2. How would you propagate a request ID in logs? → CallId plugin plus MDC; for coroutines add MDCContext (Q225).
  3. Netty vs CIO? → Netty is the battle-tested default for production; CIO is pure Kotlin and lighter, verify feature support (HTTP/2, etc.) for your version.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Handlers are suspend." Senior discusses lifecycle scopes, engine threads, client reuse, shutdown ordering and timeouts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An HttpClient created per request leaked connections until the pod ran out of file descriptors at ~65k.

questions.promptHtml: Why does SLF4J MDC lose its values across coroutine suspension points, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Observability is non-negotiable on a server, and MDC is the classic ThreadLocal-meets-coroutines trap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: MDC is a ThreadLocal. A coroutine can suspend on one thread and resume on another, so the values stay behind or, worse, a different request's values are visible. The fix is MDCContext from kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j, a ThreadContextElement that copies the MDC map into the thread each time the coroutine resumes and restores the old state when it suspends. Children inherit it through the coroutine context.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• ThreadContextElement has updateThreadContext (runs before resume, returns old state) and restoreThreadContext (runs after suspend). The infrastructure keeps the state between calls. This is the general mechanism for any ThreadLocal.
  • MDCContext() captures the MDC at creation. If you create it in a handler after setting the request ID, all child coroutines see it.
  • MDC changes made inside the coroutine (e.g. MDC.put("userId", ...)) are restored when the coroutine suspends, so they do not leak to the next coroutine on that thread, but they are also not saved back into the element by default. To update, use withContext(MDCContext()) again after the put.
  • Cost: a map copy at each resume. Fine for request-level, avoid in hot inner loops.
  • Raw ThreadLocals: threadLocal.asContextElement(value).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun handle(requestId: String) {
    MDC.put("requestId", requestId)
    withContext(MDCContext()) {                 // captures current MDC
        log.info("start")                        // has requestId
        val r = async(Dispatchers.IO) { log.info("db"); query() }.await()  // inherits
        log.info("done $r")
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting MDC then launching without MDCContext: child logs lack the ID.
  • Calling MDC.put inside the coroutine and expecting it in a sibling.
  • Supplying a fresh MDCContext() deep in the call tree after MDC was already cleared: it captures the empty map and overrides the good one.
  • Forgetting the slf4j module dependency.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not use InheritableThreadLocal? → It copies at thread creation, not at resume; pooled threads would have stale values.
  2. Is the MDC value visible in finally after cancellation? → Yes, the element still applies when the coroutine resumes to run the finally block.
  3. What about Logback's async appender? → The MDC is captured at the logging call, so it works once MDC is correct at that point.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use MDCContext." Senior explains the update/restore mechanism, per-resume cost, how to update values, and why ThreadLocal state in general is hazardous in coroutine code.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Logs for one customer showed another customer's ID in a multi-tenant system because a hand-rolled MDC copy ran only once per request, not per resume.

questions.contextHtml: A Spring Boot + Kotlin service on WebFlux (6 pods, 4 vCPU, ~1,800 RPS). After a refactor that introduced withContext(Dispatchers.IO) for a legacy DAO, support reports two problems: (1) about 12% of log lines have no traceId, and these cluster around DB calls; (2) in audit logs, a handful of entries carry a userId belonging to a different user. Security is alarmed. The code sets MDC.put("userId", u) in a WebFilter and reads SecurityContextHolder.getContext() in a service method after withContext(IO). Heap and GC are normal; no errors in logs.
questions.promptHtml: How do you explain these symptoms, stop the leak of wrong userIds, and make it robust?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Probably a logging config issue" or "add synchronized". It does not link ThreadLocal state to thread switches and pooled threads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where exactly is MDC set (filter vs handler)? Is MDCContext/PropagationContextElement anywhere? Is the user ID used for authorization decisions or only logging? Do bad logs correlate with the Dispatchers.IO section? Since when (which deploy)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: First, make sure authorization does not read SecurityContextHolder after thread hops; if it does, that is a security incident, so hotfix by passing the principal explicitly as a parameter. Then roll back the refactor if the fix is not minutes away.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) MDC ThreadLocal not propagated into IO threads, which explains missing traceId; (b) MDC set on a pooled thread and never cleared, so a later request on that thread sees stale userId; (c) SecurityContext ThreadLocal empty/stale on IO thread; (d) Reactor Context vs ThreadLocal mismatch; (e) logging backend bug (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce locally with parallel k6 requests and two users; log Thread.currentThread().name plus MDC at each step; grep prod logs for rows where thread name is DefaultDispatcher-worker-* and traceId absent; write a test that asserts MDC after withContext(IO).
  5. Root cause: MDC and SecurityContext are ThreadLocals. withContext(IO) resumes on pooled worker threads; nothing copied the values. Separately the filter put userId into a thread's MDC and never removed it, so the next coroutine that ran on that thread (with no MDC of its own) read the previous user's value.
  6. Fix: Short-term: pass principal explicitly. Long-term: add MDCContext() where the request coroutine begins; for tracing add PropagationContextElement() (Micrometer context-propagation) or enable Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation(); use ReactiveSecurityContextHolder / awaitSingle for security in WebFlux; never MDC.put without a matching MDC.clear() in a finally.
suspend fun withRequestContext(userId: String, block: suspend () -> Unit) {
    MDC.put("userId", userId)
    try { withContext(MDCContext() + PropagationContextElement()) { block() } }
    finally { MDC.remove("userId") }
}
  1. Prevention: A test fixture that runs two users concurrently and asserts logs; a Detekt/ArchUnit rule against bare MDC.put outside a helper; authorization must never depend on ThreadLocals in suspend code.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make ThreadLocals "sticky" by pinning to one thread. The per-resume copy cost of MDCContext is small versus the safety.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can MDCContext itself leak? → It restores the previous state after each suspend, so no, as long as the code outside also cleans up.
  • What if a library creates its own threads? → Capture context explicitly (MDC.getCopyOfContextMap) and set it in the task wrapper.
  • Which one is worse, missing or wrong userId? → Wrong: it is a compliance incident, not just a debugging nuisance.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An audit trail attributed an admin action to a regular user for three weeks. Root cause was one un-cleared MDC.put in a filter and a pool of 32 worker threads.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames logging library; cannot explain thread hop.
  • Hire: identifies ThreadLocal vs coroutine resume and uses MDCContext.
  • Strong hire: separates security incident from observability, explains stale pooled-thread state, adds tests and guards.

questions.promptHtml: Besides MDC, which other thread-bound things break inside coroutines on a server (security context, tracing spans, JPA/JDBC transactions), and how do you handle each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows if you understand that "thread = unit of context" assumption underpins most Java frameworks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Anything stored in a ThreadLocal is unsafe across suspension: Spring's SecurityContextHolder, @Transactional (it binds a connection to a thread), tracing spans in Micrometer/OpenTelemetry. Per resume the dispatcher may pick another thread. Fixes: use a coroutine-aware mechanism. Tracing: PropagationContextElement or OTel's coroutine context extension. Security: reactive security context. Transactions: TransactionalOperator.executeAndAwait on reactive stack; with blocking JDBC keep the whole transaction inside one withContext(Dispatchers.IO) block without suspension.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Blocking transaction: @Transactional binds the JDBC connection to the thread in a ThreadLocal via TransactionSynchronizationManager. Suspend functions can resume elsewhere, so the second statement may run with no transaction or another connection. Safe pattern: do the whole transaction as a single blocking lambda on one IO thread; no suspend calls inside.
  • Reactive transactions (R2DBC) store state in the Reactor Context; Spring's coroutine helpers (executeAndAwait) bridge it.
  • Tracing: Spring docs name PropagationContextElement (needs io.micrometer:context-propagation) so log lines from suspend code keep traceId. OTel has a Kotlin extension (asContextElement); verify the artifact for your version.
  • Security: in WebFlux the principal is in the Reactor Context; in suspend code read it with awaitSingleOrNull on ReactiveSecurityContextHolder, or pass the principal explicitly.
  • General helper: ThreadLocal.asContextElement(value).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Blocking JDBC transaction: one thread, no suspension inside
suspend fun transfer(a: Long, b: Long, amt: BigDecimal) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    txTemplate.execute {                 // TransactionTemplate, thread-bound
        accounts.debit(a, amt)           // blocking calls only, never suspend/await here
        accounts.credit(b, amt)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• @Transactional on a suspend function with JPA: transaction can be lost after the first suspension.
  • runBlocking inside a transaction template to call a suspend function: pins a thread and may deadlock.
  • Reading SecurityContextHolder after a dispatcher change.
  • Forgetting that async children inside a transaction run on other threads and do not share the transaction.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can two async blocks share one DB transaction? → Not on blocking JDBC; a connection is single-threaded for a transaction and thread-bound by Spring. Serialize or use one connection explicitly.
  2. How do you test it? → Integration test that interleaves two requests and asserts rollback.
  3. How does this change under virtual threads? → Thread-per-request returns, ThreadLocals work again (with their memory costs); see Q233.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows MDC. Senior lists transactions, security, tracing, and gives the safe patterns per stack (blocking vs reactive).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A payment transfer committed the debit but not the credit when a suspend call in the middle resumed on a different thread and ran with auto-commit.

questions.promptHtml: A client closes the connection while your handler is waiting on three downstream calls and a DB query. What happens in a coroutine-based server, and what do you have to do for cancellation to be effective?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cancellation saves real money under load (wasted work during retries and timeouts) and it is easy to break.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If the engine/framework detects the disconnect it cancels the request coroutine's Job, and cancellation propagates to children. But cancellation is cooperative: a suspend call that is cancellable (delay, Ktor client, await) throws CancellationException at the suspension point. Blocking code does not stop. So I make downstream calls cancellable, never swallow CancellationException, and for blocking JDBC I use statement timeouts or runInterruptible.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Framework side: reactive path in Spring cancels the subscription which cancels the coroutine. In Ktor, behavior depends on the engine and version; verify that the call coroutine is cancelled on disconnect in your engine. For MVC, a servlet client abort is detected only when writing.
  • Cooperative: isActive checks, or any suspending function from kotlinx.coroutines (all are cancellable), checks the Job. A CPU loop without suspension points ignores cancellation: add ensureActive() or yield().
  • Blocking calls: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { jdbc } keeps running after cancel; the result is discarded. runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { blocking } turns cancellation into Thread.interrupt, which works for interruptible waits (sleep, some socket/NIO channels, BlockingQueue) but not plain socket reads or JDBC unless the driver honours it. For JDBC use statement.setQueryTimeout and statement.cancel() in invokeOnCompletion.
  • Cleanup after cancel: suspend calls in finally throw immediately because the Job is cancelled; wrap in withContext(NonCancellable).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun report(): Report = coroutineScope {
    val a = async { clientA.get() }          // cancellable HTTP
    val b = async { clientB.get() }
    val rows = runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { dao.heavyQuery() } // interrupt on cancel
    Report(a.await(), b.await(), rows)
}
// cleanup
try { work() } finally { withContext(NonCancellable) { audit.log("aborted") } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• catch (e: Exception) swallowing CancellationException (see Q229).
  • Assuming withContext(IO) stops the query.
  • Cleanup in finally using suspend calls without NonCancellable.
  • A CPU loop with no suspension point.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does cancelling a parent cancel async children? → Yes, structured concurrency.
  2. Does cancelling the request coroutine cancel a GlobalScope.launch? → No, which is why it is an antipattern.
  3. How do you stop a 30 s Postgres query? → Statement cancel() (server-side cancel) and setQueryTimeout; interrupting the thread alone is not enough with most drivers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Cancellation propagates." Senior: cooperativeness, blocking code limits, runInterruptible, NonCancellable cleanup, and engine-specific detection.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reporting endpoint kept running 10-minute queries after users navigated away; retries stacked up until the DB hit max connections.

questions.contextHtml:
A Ktor service with a pricing endpoint has a timeout of 2 s at the gateway. At 500 RPS, during a downstream slowdown, the DB shows ~300 active sessions running the pricing query although gateway timeouts return 504 to users. Pod memory grows 400 MB over an hour. Code:

suspend fun quote(id: String): Quote {
    return try {
        withTimeout(2_000) {
            val base = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { dao.basePrice(id) }   // blocking JDBC
            val fx = fxClient.rate(base.currency)                          // suspend, Ktor client
            Quote(base, fx)
        }
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        log.warn("quote failed", e)
        Quote.fallback(id)
    } finally {
        metrics.record(id)                    // suspend call
    }
}

Logs show TimeoutCancellationException stack traces logged as warnings, and also callers that cancelled still returning fallback quotes.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with this code and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase timeout" or "add try/catch for Timeout". Misses the swallowed CancellationException, uncancellable blocking JDBC and the suspend call in finally.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which driver and does it support query timeout? Is the gateway timeout the same as the service timeout? What does metrics.record do? Is quote called inside other scopes (e.g. fan-out)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set statement timeout at the DB role level (e.g. Postgres statement_timeout), lower concurrency limit, kill long sessions via pg_cancel_backend.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) catch (e: Exception) catches TimeoutCancellationException (a CancellationException) so the coroutine treats cancellation as failure and keeps going: a cancelled caller still gets a fallback; (b) withContext(IO) blocking JDBC continues after timeout, result dropped; (c) suspend metrics.record in finally on a cancelled coroutine throws immediately; (d) memory growth: pending results from threads still running (red herring partly: also unbounded retries).
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_activity for session age and query text; a unit test with runTest that cancels the job and asserts the DAO was interrupted; thread dump; heap histogram jcmd GC.class_histogram.
  5. Root cause: Catching Exception swallows cancellation, breaking the cooperative contract; blocking JDBC ignores cancellation; the finally block's suspend call is run in a cancelled coroutine so it throws CancellationException and the metric is lost.
  6. Fix:
suspend fun quote(id: String): Quote = try {
    withTimeout(2_000) {
        val base = runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { dao.basePrice(id) } // + setQueryTimeout(2) in dao
        Quote(base, fxClient.rate(base.currency))
    }
} catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) {
    Quote.fallback(id)                       // only the deadline we own
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e                                  // caller cancelled: never swallow
} catch (e: Exception) {
    log.warn("quote failed", e); Quote.fallback(id)
} finally {
    withContext(NonCancellable) { metrics.record(id) }
}

Note: TimeoutCancellationException from our own withTimeout is safe to handle because it is thrown outside the block; an outer cancellation must be rethrown. Prefer withTimeoutOrNull. 7. Prevention: Detekt rule SuspendFunSwallowedCancellation; code review checklist; runCatching banned in suspend code (it catches CancellationException); DB-level statement_timeout. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove the fallback; I would not rely on thread interrupt for JDBC without verifying the driver (pgjdbc honours Statement.cancel() better than interrupt).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is runCatching dangerous? → It catches CancellationException too.
  • What if the DAO is called inside async and one fails? → sibling cancellation, covered in Q230.
  • Is TimeoutCancellationException an Exception you should log at warn? → Usually info/metric; log level matters at 500 RPS.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 3 s DB timeout was "enforced" by withTimeout but the queries ran to completion, so a retry storm turned a slow dependency into a DB outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sees nothing wrong or suggests longer timeout.
  • Hire: spots swallowed CancellationException and non-cancellable JDBC.
  • Strong hire: also NonCancellable finally, statement timeouts, the distinction between own timeout and outer cancellation, and guards.

questions.promptHtml: How do you call three services in parallel from a request handler with coroutines, and what happens if one of them fails?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic daily task; the interesting part is failure semantics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: coroutineScope { val a = async { ... }; val b = async { ... }; ... }. The scope waits for all children, and if one throws, the scope cancels the siblings and rethrows. If I want partial results I use supervisorScope (children fail independently) and handle exceptions per await.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• coroutineScope creates a child scope of the caller; the caller suspends until all children complete. Cancellation of the request propagates in.
  • Failure: a failing async fails its parent scope, which cancels the other children; coroutineScope rethrows the first exception.
  • supervisorScope: a child's failure does not cancel siblings; exception is raised only at await(). For launch children inside a supervisor scope, uncaught exceptions go to the CoroutineExceptionHandler.
  • async outside a scope (e.g. GlobalScope) breaks structure: no cancellation, orphaned exceptions.
  • Concurrency is bounded by the dispatcher; for large lists use a Semaphore or limitedParallelism to avoid thousands of concurrent calls (see Q232).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun dashboard(id: String) = supervisorScope {
    val user = async { users.get(id) }
    val orders = async { orders.list(id) }
    val recs = async { runCatching { recs.get(id) }.getOrNull() } // optional, degrade
    Dashboard(user.await(), orders.await(), recs.await())
}

(Use runCatching carefully: it also catches cancellation; prefer an explicit try/catch that rethrows CancellationException.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• try { async { } } catch outside the scope: exception surfaces at the scope, not at async.
  • supervisorScope with launch and no handler: failures only logged.
  • Starting async and forgetting await (errors lost or reported late).
  • coroutineScope expecting siblings to continue after failure.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. coroutineScope vs CoroutineScope(...)? → The first is a suspending scope bound to the caller; the second creates an unmanaged scope you must cancel yourself.
  2. awaitAll vs map { it.await() }? → awaitAll fails fast on first failure; sequential awaits wait in order.
  3. How to return the first successful result? → select/channels or race via Channel and cancel others; verify cancellation of losers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "async/await". Senior: failure semantics, supervisor trade-off, bounding concurrency, never GlobalScope, and exception handler placement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard endpoint returned 500 whenever the recommendations service blipped, because a coroutineScope cancelled the healthy user and order calls; making recs optional via supervisorScope restored availability.

questions.contextHtml: A product-page endpoint at 1,200 RPS fans out to 4 services: catalog (p99 40 ms, required), price (p99 60 ms, required), reviews (p99 300 ms, optional), recs (p99 800 ms, optional, occasionally 5 s). The SLO is p99 under 400 ms. Today a sequential implementation has p99 1.2 s. Product wants "always show something". A teammate proposes one withTimeout(400) around the whole fan-out.
questions.promptHtml: Design the fan-out, timeouts and degradation. What would you do about overload?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Parallelize everything with one global timeout; failure of any optional call returns a 500 or the whole page times out.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which fields are mandatory for rendering? Is stale data acceptable (cache)? Are downstreams idempotent/safe to hedge? What is the retry policy upstream? Is there already a circuit breaker library?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (not an incident) Ship parallel fan-out with per-call budgets before anything else; that alone drops p99 to roughly max of required calls.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Latency is dominated by recs and reviews in sequence (800 + 300 + 100 = 1.2 s). A single global timeout would keep p99 at 400 ms but kill required data when optional calls are slow.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test with k6 injecting a 5 s recs tail; measure p99 and error rate; Micrometer timers per dependency.
  5. Root cause / design: Required calls get a budget slightly above p99 (e.g. 150 ms) and fail the request; optional calls get a hard budget derived from the SLO remainder (e.g. reviews 250 ms, recs 250 ms) and degrade to null.
  6. Fix:
suspend fun page(id: String) = supervisorScope {
    val catalog = async { withTimeout(150) { catalogClient.get(id) } }
    val price   = async { withTimeout(150) { priceClient.get(id) } }
    val reviews = async { withTimeoutOrNull(250) { reviewsClient.get(id) } }
    val recs    = async { withTimeoutOrNull(250) { recsClient.get(id) } }
    Page(catalog.await(), price.await(), reviews.await(), recs.await())
}

Note: withTimeoutOrNull returns null on timeout but other exceptions still propagate at await; wrap optional calls with a function that logs and returns null for non-cancellation errors. In supervisorScope, when a required call fails, await throws; I must cancel the optional siblings by letting the exception exit the scope. 7. Prevention: Per-dependency timers and error budgets; a feature flag to disable optional blocks; cache recs for 5 minutes (stale-while-revalidate). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use one timeout for everything. I would not retry optional calls (it amplifies tail latency). Hedging only for idempotent reads with a budget, accepting extra load of maybe 5-10%.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Downstream is slow, not failing: do timeouts help? → They bound latency but queues of in-flight calls grow; add a circuit breaker and bulkhead (Q232).
  • What if withTimeout fires after the response is already built? → It is scoped to the call; cancellation of a completed child is a no-op.
  • Does timeout cancel the HTTP call? → With Ktor/WebClient, yes the call is cancelled; with blocking clients it is not (Q228).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A global 1 s timeout meant a slow optional widget took the entire homepage down once a week; splitting budgets turned it into a missing carousel.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sequential or single timeout.
  • Hire: parallel with per-call budgets and optional degradation.
  • Strong hire: budgets derived from SLO and p99s, no retries on optional, circuit breaker/bulkhead, caching, and cancellation realities.

questions.promptHtml: How would you implement bulkheads and concurrency limits per downstream dependency using coroutines, and when do you use a Semaphore versus limitedParallelism?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who only parallelize from people who protect the system from slow dependencies.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A bulkhead caps concurrent in-flight calls per dependency so one slow service cannot eat all capacity. Use a Semaphore(n) for non-blocking suspend calls: coroutines waiting for a permit suspend cheaply, and permits are held across suspension. Use limitedParallelism(n) for blocking calls, since it limits threads actually running. Add a bounded wait (timeout on acquire) so queues cannot grow forever, and fail fast when full.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Little's law: in-flight = throughput x latency. If recs goes from 50 ms to 5 s at 200 RPS, in-flight rises from 10 to 1,000. With coroutines each is cheap (hundreds of bytes to a few KB), so memory is rarely the first limit; the downstream, sockets and connection pools are.
  • Semaphore: withPermit holds a permit while the coroutine is suspended on the network call. Right tool for HTTP clients.
  • limitedParallelism: holds a slot only while running on a thread. Wrong for non-blocking calls (a suspended coroutine does not hold the slot, so no limiting happens), right for blocking JDBC/SDKs.
  • Queue bound: withTimeout(50) { sem.acquire() } to shed load instead of piling up; or tryAcquire() for immediate reject.
  • Adjacent: circuit breaker (Resilience4j has Kotlin coroutine extensions; verify module and version), rate limiter, and the HTTP client's own connection pool limit (Ktor CIO maxConnectionsCount, verify).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Bulkhead(permits: Int, private val waitMs: Long) {
    private val sem = Semaphore(permits)
    suspend fun <T> call(block: suspend () -> T): T {
        val got = withTimeoutOrNull(waitMs) { sem.acquire(); true } ?: throw BulkheadFullException()
        try { return block() } finally { sem.release() }
    }
}
class BulkheadFullException : RuntimeException()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using limitedParallelism to limit HTTP calls: no effect during suspension.
  • Unbounded wait for a permit: queues grow and latency becomes the timeout.
  • Releasing permit incorrectly on cancellation (use try/finally; kotlinx withPermit does this).
  • One shared semaphore for all dependencies: defeats isolation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you choose n? → Little's law with p99 and target RPS, capped by downstream capacity divided by number of pods.
  2. How is it different from a rate limiter? → Bulkhead limits concurrency; rate limiter limits arrivals per second.
  3. What do you return when full? → Fail fast with fallback or 503 with Retry-After, never queue unbounded.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use Semaphore." Senior: chooses between Semaphore and dispatcher views, bounds the wait, derives n, and combines with timeouts/circuit breakers and per-pod division of limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A single slow partner API absorbed all 64 IO slots and 2k suspended coroutines, killing unrelated endpoints until per-dependency limits were added.

questions.promptHtml: On JDK 21+, why would you still use Kotlin coroutines on a server instead of just virtual threads, and when would you pick virtual threads?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests judgement on a live architectural debate, without tribalism.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both give cheap concurrency, but they sit at different layers. Virtual threads (final in Java 21) make blocking code scale with zero code changes, but give no structured concurrency or built-in cancellation semantics beyond interrupts (structured concurrency in the JDK is still a preview API, verify for your version). Coroutines give explicit suspension, structured concurrency, cancellation, Flow and dispatcher control. For a mostly blocking JDBC service I'd lean to virtual threads; for Kotlin-first code with heavy fan-out, cancellation and Flow I'd keep coroutines, and they can be combined.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect Coroutines Virtual threads (JDK 21)
Implemented by compiler (state machine) + library JVM scheduler (continuations on ForkJoinPool carriers)
Blocking JDBC blocks a pool thread; must offload unmounts on blocking IO, fine
Cancellation cooperative, structured interrupt() only
ThreadLocals broken across resumes, need context elements work (memory per thread cost)
Pinning not applicable (no carrier pinning) synchronized blocks with blocking inside pin carrier in 21; JEP 491 addresses this in JDK 24 (verify)
Language Kotlin only any JVM language
  • Virtual threads still need limits: 10k virtual threads can hammer a 20-connection DB pool. Concurrency bounds (Semaphore) remain necessary.
  • Interop: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() lets coroutines run blocking code on virtual threads, replacing Dispatchers.IO for blocking sections. Verify available APIs in your kotlinx.coroutines version; newer versions may offer more direct support.
  • Debuggability: virtual threads show up in thread dumps (jcmd Thread.dump_to_file), coroutines need the debug agent/DebugProbes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()
suspend fun legacy(id: Long) = withContext(vt) { blockingDao.find(id) } // blocking OK here

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring one "dead": they solve overlapping, not identical, problems.
  • Believing virtual threads remove the need for timeouts/bulkheads.
  • Pooling virtual threads (defeats the purpose).
  • Ignoring pinning on JDK 21 with synchronized + blocking IO.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you cancel a virtual thread's blocking JDBC call? → Only via interrupt/driver cancel, same limits as Q228.
  2. Does Spring support both? → Spring Boot 3.2+ can use virtual threads via spring.threads.virtual.enabled (verify); coroutines via reactor support.
  3. Would you rewrite a coroutine service? → No, not unless a measured problem exists.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Virtual threads are the new coroutines." Senior compares along cancellation, structure, ThreadLocals, pinning, language and team skills, and cites the combination option.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team moved to virtual threads and saw DB connection pool exhaustion because concurrency was no longer implicitly bounded by a thread pool size.

questions.contextHtml: A Kotlin Spring MVC service (JDK 17, Tomcat 200 threads, JPA/Hibernate, HikariCP 30) handles 900 RPS. Calls to a slow partner (p50 200 ms, p99 3 s) cause Tomcat threads to saturate during partner incidents (all 200 busy, queue grows, 503s). Management asks to "go reactive/coroutines" in one quarter. The team has 4 engineers and 40% of the code uses JPA lazy loading and @Transactional.
questions.promptHtml: What do you propose, and how do you migrate with live traffic?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite everything to WebFlux with coroutines" without regard to JPA, or "just double Tomcat threads."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the pain the partner call only, or all endpoints? Can we move to JDK 21? What is the actual bottleneck: threads, DB pool, or CPU? What's the team's coroutine experience? Is the partner idempotent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Bulkhead and timeout the partner call (Resilience4j/semaphore, 800 ms timeout), separate executor for it so other endpoints keep threads, return fallback.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Threads blocked on the partner (200 x 3 s tail); DB pool not the limit (30); CPU low. Options: (A) full WebFlux/R2DBC rewrite; (B) JDK 21 + virtual threads in Tomcat; (C) keep MVC, make only the partner leg coroutine/async.
  4. How I'd verify each: Thread dumps during incident; Micrometer tomcat.threads.busy; load test with a simulated slow partner; check driver and library pinning (-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full) on JDK 21.
  5. Root cause: Thread-per-request capacity equals thread count; slow dependency converts to thread exhaustion by Little's law (900 RPS x 3 s tail on a slice = hundreds of threads).
  6. Fix: I recommend B plus bulkhead: upgrade to JDK 21, enable virtual threads for request handling (Spring Boot 3.2+, verify flag), keep JPA and @Transactional unchanged since ThreadLocals still work, and cap partner concurrency with a Semaphore at about 100. Use coroutines only in new code that benefits from structured fan-out. Rollout: canary 5% of pods, compare p99, errors, DB pool pending, then 25/50/100%; keep a flag to revert to platform threads.
  7. Prevention: Per-dependency metrics, load test of partner slowness in CI, pinning detection in staging.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rewrite JPA to R2DBC in a quarter: high risk, lazy loading and transactions semantics change. I would not enable virtual threads without raising awareness that the DB pool (30) becomes the new limit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if we cannot move off JDK 17? → Keep platform threads, bulkhead the partner leg with a dedicated pool, or use coroutines with withContext for just that call.
  • Pinning risk? → On 21, synchronized around blocking IO pins; check libraries; JEP 491 (JDK 24) reduces this, verify.
  • Isn't reactive more scalable? → For pure IO fan-out with huge connection counts, yes; but the cost is complexity and mismatch with JPA.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "reactive rewrite" estimated at 6 months was replaced by a two-week bulkhead plus JDK upgrade that fixed 90% of incidents.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: pushes rewrite or only more threads.
  • Hire: bulkhead + choose virtual threads or partial coroutines with reasons.
  • Strong hire: quantifies via Little's law, plans canary with metrics, identifies DB pool as the next limit, and states fallback.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test suspend code on the server deterministically, including delays, timeouts and dispatcher usage?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Flaky Thread.sleep tests are a smell; they want to see you know virtual time and dispatcher injection.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use runTest from kotlinx-coroutines-test. It runs the body with a test scheduler and skips delay in virtual time, so a 2-second timeout test runs instantly. I inject dispatchers into classes instead of hard-coding Dispatchers.IO, pass the test dispatcher, and use advanceTimeBy/runCurrent to step through. For real blocking calls I use a real dispatcher in integration tests.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• runTest creates a TestScope with a StandardTestDispatcher (queues coroutines until you advance or the test body suspends). UnconfinedTestDispatcher runs eagerly, useful for simple tests but can hide ordering bugs.
  • Virtual time applies only to the test scheduler. If code uses Dispatchers.IO internally, delay there is real time, so inject dispatchers.
  • Timeouts: withTimeout uses the scheduler's delay under runTest, so you can assert a call times out at exactly 2,000 ms of virtual time.
  • runTest has its own timeout in real time (10 s by default in recent versions; verify) to catch hangs.
  • Leaked coroutines: runTest fails if children are still running at the end (structured concurrency helps).
  • Cancellation: test by launching, advanceUntilIdle, job.cancel(), then assert cleanup ran.
  • Integration: Testcontainers for real DB; BlockHound for blocking detection.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class QuoteService(private val io: CoroutineDispatcher, private val fx: FxClient) {
    suspend fun quote(id: String) = withTimeoutOrNull(2_000) { withContext(io) { fx.rate(id) } }
}

@Test fun timesOut() = runTest {
    val slow = FxClient { delay(5_000); 1.0 }
    val svc = QuoteService(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler), slow)
    val result = svc.quote("EUR")
    assertNull(result)
    assertEquals(2_000, currentTime)       // virtual time
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hard-coding Dispatchers.IO inside the class, making delays real.
  • Using runBlocking in tests and Thread.sleep.
  • Forgetting Dispatchers.setMain is irrelevant on servers (only for Android/UI).
  • Using UnconfinedTestDispatcher everywhere and missing concurrency bugs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test Flow? → collect into a list inside runTest, or use Turbine (library) for step-wise assertions.
  2. How do you test that cancellation works? → cancel the job, assert finally ran and downstream called with cancel.
  3. How do you test a Semaphore bulkhead? → launch n+1 coroutines with test dispatcher, assert the last waits until a permit is released.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "runBlocking and sleep". Senior: virtual time, injected dispatchers, explicit cancellation tests, and complement with integration tests and BlockHound.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Flaky CI from timing-based tests hid a real race; moving to runTest exposed an ordering bug on first run.

questions.contextHtml:
A notification service (Kotlin, Ktor, 3 pods, 2 GB heap each) slowly degrades. Over 6 days, heap use climbs from 600 MB to 1.7 GB; at day 6 pods hit OOM and restart, then the cycle repeats. Threads dumps show 4,000+ idle DefaultDispatcher-worker entries are not the issue (only 64), but a heap dump (Eclipse MAT) shows ~1.1 M StandaloneCoroutine objects, each holding references to request payloads. Code review reveals:

class Notifier(private val sender: Sender) {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO)
    fun enqueue(n: Notification) { scope.launch { sender.send(n) } }   // called per request
}

sender.send has no timeout; the email provider occasionally hangs connections for minutes. Also a GlobalScope.launch in a retry helper.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: root cause, fixes, and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap to 4 GB" or "memory leak in Ktor". It misses unbounded fire-and-forget work and missing timeouts.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the enqueue rate vs send rate? Is the provider slower lately? Does a restart lose notifications (durability)? How does shutdown behave? Are other scopes created per request?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart pods on a schedule or lower the heap threshold to keep serving; add a timeout (withTimeout(10_000)) and a hard cap on in-flight sends by hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Unbounded launch per request with slow/hung send accumulating coroutines (arrival rate > completion rate); (b) SupervisorJob scope never cancelled, so completed children are removed but hung ones stay; (c) GlobalScope retry loop holding payloads; (d) Ktor leak (red herring, heap shows coroutines).
  4. How I'd verify each: MAT dominator tree and "path to GC roots" of StandaloneCoroutine; jcmd GC.class_histogram; kotlinx-coroutines DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() to see suspension points (all in send socket read); metric of in-flight sends.
  5. Root cause: A fire-and-forget scope with no backpressure and no timeouts: when the provider hangs 5 minutes at 300 enq/s that is 90,000 live coroutines per provider stall (300 x 300 s); repeated stalls accumulate payload references. No limit means memory is the limit.
  6. Fix: Replace with a bounded Channel plus fixed workers (backpressure), timeout per send, and drop-or-persist when full. Persist to a queue (Kafka/SQS) for durability.
class Notifier(private val sender: Sender, scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val ch = Channel<Notification>(capacity = 1_000)   // bounded
    init { repeat(16) { scope.launch { for (n in ch) runCatchingNonCancel { withTimeout(10_000) { sender.send(n) } } } } }
    suspend fun enqueue(n: Notification) = ch.trySend(n).isSuccess  // false => shed/persist
}

(runCatchingNonCancel is a helper that rethrows CancellationException but, TimeoutCancellationException from the inner timeout must be caught first.) Scope is owned by the application and cancelled on ApplicationStopping. 7. Prevention: Alert on coroutine count (DebugProbes in staging or a custom gauge of in-flight work), heap growth slope alerts, Detekt GlobalCoroutineUsage, mandatory timeouts on all outbound calls, load test with a hanging provider. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not bump the heap. Bounded channel means shedding; that decision (drop vs persist) is a product decision I'd confirm.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why are the coroutines cheap yet this still OOMs? → They hold payloads and request objects; 1.1M x ~1 KB is already 1.1 GB.
  • Does SupervisorJob accumulate completed children? → No, completed children are removed; hung ones accumulate.
  • How should shutdown behave? → Close the channel, drain with a timeout, cancel the scope.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "harmless" fire-and-forget audit logger took the service down at 3 AM because the audit store slowed; the fix was a ten-line bounded channel.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases heap, blames framework.
  • Hire: finds unbounded launches and missing timeouts, uses bounded channel.
  • Strong hire: quantifies accumulation rate, uses heap dump and DebugProbes, addresses durability, shutdown and guard rails.
